foreground.title: Idaho Dairy Industry's Vulnerability to Long-Term Drought
foreground.subtitle: Alycia Bean, University of Idaho, Geography Department A presentation for the 2018 Innovation Showcase

text.value: The dairy industry in Idaho is booming.
It has grown tenfold since the late 1980s.
Along with the growth of the dairy industry is the commodity increase in milk production  - the largest agricultural sector in Idaho with a 2016 value of $2.36 billion (NASS, 2017)
Idaho ranks first in the U.S. for production of certified organic hay, and is the second largest U.S. producer of alfalfa hay.
Alfalfa makes up more than 80% of Idaho’s total hay production, with over  4 million tons harvested per year (Idaho State Department of Agriculture).
While alfalfa is a profitable crop and needed to support the growing dairy industry, it is a very water intensive crop at an average of 46 inches of water per growing season (Shewmaker et al., 2013).
Water in alfalfa country in southern Idaho is already over allocated.
In fact, in a good water year, there is not enough water for all needs in the Magic Valley in southern Idaho.

Junior water users in the hierarchy of 'first in time, first in line' have already (2015) agreed to cut their consumptive use by ~13% so senior (often surface water users) can have their full water rights fulfilled.
Climate change is anticipated to increase surface and air temperature in the semi-arid region of southern Idaho (Abatzoglou, 2014).
With an increase in temperature comes an increase in evapotranspiration (ET), meaning even more thirsty alfalfa crops.
The estimated ET of alfalfa is between 36 - 55 inches per crop (Hansen, 2015).

title.value: Overview of Interdisciplinary Data Collected and Questions Asked

text.value: The Magic Valley is defined as the six counties of Cassia, Gooding, Jerome, Lincoln, Minidoka, and Twin Falls along the Snake River and above the Eastern Snake Plain Aquifer (ESPA).
The Magic Valley of southern Idaho is home to a wide variety of irrigated agriculture and all of Idaho's alfalfa growth.
This image shows USDA National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS) cropland cover in the Magic Valley.
The green in this image represents the alfalfa farms reported to the  NASS and is extracted from the most recent cropland data layer in 2016.
Each pixel represents a            30 x 30m area.
A water right is the right to divert the public waters of the state of Idaho and put them to a beneficial use, in accordance with one’s priority date.
Water Right Permits:  The POU is the legal location where you use your water right.
Water Right Permits:  A POD is the legal location where you divert water from its source

title.value: What type of Water Right do they have?

text.value: The assumption that a particular water right is used for an alfalfa crop is based on the following true statements:
1. The IDWR permitted right is of the type of Water Use category: “Irrigation”, “Irrigation from storage”, or “Irrigation storage”
that water right overlaps with a NASS Cropland Data Layer pixel for the category “alfalfa”.
2. The IDWR permitted right is within 100 meters (creating a 200m diameter)  of a NASS reported alfalfa crop pixel (at 30x30m grid, based on the most recent CDL, 2016).
- Limitations within query itself and sources of data acquisition.

text.value: Since 2000, Idaho has declared drought nearly 150 times (IDWR, 2017), almost every year (minus 06, 09, 11).
In 2015 all of Idaho was in a drought (Idaho State Drought Monitor Report).

For the semi-arid region in southern Idaho, the maximum temperature and the potential evapotranspiration are projected through 2080 showing an increase in both variables despite the emissions scenarios (Image Credit: The Northwest Climate Toolbox).

Additionally, peak runoff of snowmelt in northwest streams is occurring about a month earlier than the historical average (Dudley et al. 2017) . The lack of storage as snow and already full reservoirs has implications of increased sensitivity to future warming (Qualls 2013).
(Image Credit: The Northwest Climate Toolbox).
There is evidence that the dairy industry in Idaho is vulnerable to long-term drought given that:
1. There may be an increase in alfalfa farms to keep up with the booming dairy industry. According to NASS, 29 crops changed to alfalfa in 2016 in the Magic Valley (for a total of 373,164 acres).

2. There is an increase in temperature and evapotranspiration (ET). Drought may occur with greater frequency and magnitude given the current warming trends (Hamlet and Lettenmaier, 2007; Pagano and Garen, 2005).

3. There is not an increase in allocated water but a decline in natural water storage such as snow pack and aquifer levels. If Magic Valley junior users are already curtailed in non-drought years, additional water supplies or more efficient water users will need to be explored to sustain growth.

In order to adequately address this issue, the climatological data (science) need to be coupled with water right allocation hierarchies (water law) to provide decision makers with information to make positive change (policy).
And that is exactly what this innovative research project is able to address.
